t.jesuit block@-31.4,-64.2:
The oldest university in Argentina is a block in the middle of Córdoba. When the Jesuits arrived in 1599 they began what became the Manzana Jesuítica, a whole city block with a church, a college and a university, and in 1613 they founded the Colegio Máximo, which developed into the Universidad Nacional de Córdoba, one of the oldest in the Americas. The Iglesia de la Compañía, begun in the 1640s and finished some decades later, has a wonderful wooden ceiling shaped like an upturned ship's hull, built by craftsmen who knew about boats, with beams of local timber joined without nails. The block, together with the Jesuit estancias in the countryside, was listed by UNESCO in 2000.

The estancias were the economic engine. These were farms and ranches run by the order, with churches, workshops and mills, which supplied the city with food and funds, and the one at Jesús María, a short drive north, now produces wine and holds a museum. Alta Gracia, in the hills south-west of the city, is another, and has the house where the young Che Guevara lived as a boy. When the Jesuits were expelled in 1767, the estancias were sold or abandoned.

Córdoba has a million and a half inhabitants and is a big, loud, student city, with fuel and parking of every kind, though the historic centre has narrow streets and heavy traffic, so give yourself time. The local drink is Fernet with cola, which is drunk everywhere, and the local food includes empanadas and a meat sandwich called lomito. Malvinas Argentinas, to the north, is a suburban town.

For riding, the Sierras de Córdoba are the pleasure. The road from Villa Carlos Paz toward Mina Clavero, called the Camino de las Altas Cumbres, climbs to high grassland over two thousand metres, with long, flowing bends, views over rocky valleys and condors circling above, and it is one of the best mountain roads in central Argentina. Wind and fog can arrive without notice, and the temperature falls sharply at the top, so wear layers. Go in autumn or spring, when the days are mild, and avoid weekends in January, when the road is crowded.
t.qanat of gowhariz@30.0,57.1:
The first thing to understand about a qanat is that you cannot see most of it. What you see here are the spoil mounds, row after row of low craters stretching up a gravel slope, each one marking a vertical shaft dug by hand to reach the tunnel beneath. The Qanat of Gowhariz belongs to the group of Persian qanats that UNESCO inscribed in 2016, and it lies in the foothills southeast of Kerman, close to the oasis town of Mahan, in a country of dry gravel fans and brown mountain walls.

A qanat is a gently sloping tunnel that taps groundwater high in the hills and lets gravity carry it, underground and out of reach of the sun, to fields and villages many kilometres away. The idea is thousands of years old and it is why people could live in places that get a few centimetres of rain a year. Gowhariz is celebrated for its depth, a well-known mother well sunk far deeper than most, and for the ingenious detail of the whole system, with its shafts, water mill sites, and the rules by which water was shared out by time rather than volume. Families owned hours of flow, and an old watch-keeper once measured them by a bowl floating in a jar.

Kerman is a bit under thirty kilometres away and is where you buy fuel and food. The road down from the city towards Mahan is wide and fast, an easy run across open desert basin, with the Jabal-Barez range along the horizon. Heat is the main variable. From June to September the middle of the day is brutal and the sensible schedule is up at dawn, finished by early afternoon. In spring the slopes can turn faintly green, and in winter the light is clear and cold, with snow often visible on the higher ridges.

Combine it with Bagh-e Shahzadeh, the Prince's Garden near Mahan, where a ribbon of water runs down terraces between cypresses and pools, which makes the underground idea suddenly visible, because the same logic of channelled water produces that green order in a bare landscape. A wide hat and a bottle you actually drink from matter more here than any piece of kit.
t.estancia of caroya@-31.0,-64.1:
The Jesuits ran their farms like small empires. In the seventeenth century the Society of Jesus built a chain of estancias around the city of Cordoba, in the centre of Argentina, which supported the university and the college in town with grain, cattle, wine and mules, and these, together with the Jesuit Block in Cordoba itself, were inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2000. The Estancia of Caroya, founded in 1616, was the first of them, and its low, thick-walled buildings, with their long arcaded gallery, courtyard and a chapel, look out over a plain bordered by the hills of the Sierras Chicas.

In 1767, the Spanish crown expelled the Jesuits from its empire, and the estancias were sold or abandoned. Caroya went through several hands, and in the late nineteenth century a new chapter began when the Argentine government settled Italian immigrants on the land, mostly families from Friuli in the north-east of Italy. Their descendants gave the district a lasting Italian character. Colonia Caroya, next to the estancia, is still known for its salami, sausages, wine and mushrooms, and in the town streets you hear Friulian accents and see vines trained over every yard.

The estancia houses a museum, with displays about the Jesuits, the workshops and the colonists, and its walls hold fragments of old paintings. A short ride away, the Estancia of Santa Catalina, on the ride's list, is the largest and most impressive of the group, with a grand church and an extensive set of buildings.

The ride from Cordoba is easy, along Route 9, a fast, smooth road heading north through flat farmland with sunflowers, maize and soy, and the hills appear to the west. Jesus Maria, with nearly twenty-seven thousand people, is a lively small city with fuel, restaurants and a famous folk festival every January, which draws crowds of music fans. The roads into the Sierras Chicas climb into hills with oaks, rock outcrops and small rivers, and are very enjoyable for a Sunday ride. Summers are hot, with heavy storms, and winters are dry and mild, so autumn and spring are the most comfortable. Try a picada, a platter of cured meats and cheese, with a glass of local red wine.
t.landscape of grand pre@45.1,-64.3:
The Bay of Fundy has the highest tides in the world, and at Grand Pré the sea comes in and out of the Minas Basin with a rush that can move the waterline across mudflats the size of a small town. Behind that shifting edge lies a broad, flat, green meadow that was not always land. The Acadians, French settlers who arrived in the seventeenth century, built earthen dykes with wooden sluice gates called aboiteaux to keep the tide out and turn salt marsh into rich farmland. The work took generations, and the dykes still protect fields today.

Grand Pré is also where one of the saddest chapters in Canadian history unfolded. In 1755, after years of conflict between Britain and France, the British authorities ordered the Acadians to be deported, and thousands were forced onto ships and scattered along the Atlantic coast and beyond. Many eventually went to Louisiana, where their descendants became known as Cajuns. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow told a fictional version of this story in his poem Evangeline in 1847, and the figure of Evangeline has become a symbol of the loss. A memorial church, a statue and gardens stand at the site, and the UNESCO listing covers the whole farmed landscape.

The ride across the Annapolis Valley is gentle, with Highway 1 and the back roads through apple orchards, vineyards and farm stands. The season matters: blossom in late May, ripe fruit and cider in September, and bright autumn colour in October. Roads are usually quiet and wide, with long views north over the basin toward Cape Blomidon, a basalt headland that glows red at sunrise. Wind off the water can be brisk, and the tide moves quickly, so keep off the mudflats.

Wolfville, only six kilometres away, has about 3,500 people and a lively main street, as it is home to Acadia University, with cafés, bakeries and the valley's wineries nearby. Kentville, 16 km off, is the larger place for fuel and supplies. The region's wine industry has grown quickly in recent years, and the cool climate suits crisp whites and sparkling styles. The long summer evening light on the dykes is the thing to wait for, and the pause here is a good one to take in quietly, as the site is a memorial as much as a view.
t.bagh e shahzadeh@30.0,57.3:
The prince who built this garden did not live to see it grow up. Bagh-e Shahzadeh, the Prince's Garden, lies near the town of Mahan, at the foot of the mountains south-east of Kerman, in a country of salt desert, gravel plains and orchards that depend entirely on water brought underground from the hills. It was laid out in the late nineteenth century for a Qajar governor of Kerman, and it is one of the nine Persian gardens that UNESCO listed together in 2011. The design is simple and strong: a long, straight axis runs up a slope from a gateway to a pavilion, with a water channel down the middle and rows of cypress and fruit trees on either side. Fountains, one after another, play in the channel, and the sound of falling water, so precious in a dry land, is the point of the whole thing.

The sloping site gives the garden its drama. As you climb, a series of terraces rises towards a pavilion at the top, with views back down the vista to the desert. Water arrives from the mountains in a qanat, a tunnel dug by hand, and the gardeners control the flow carefully. In the evening, local families come to picnic on the carpets, and the garden is full of children and chatter.

Mahan itself is best known for the shrine of Shah Nematollah Vali, a Sufi master, with turquoise domes and a quiet courtyard. Kerman, thirty-five kilometres away, is the big city, with half a million people, fuel, hotels and a lively bazaar. The Ganjali Khan complex there, a Safavid-era group of bathhouse, caravanserai and market, is a fine place to spend an afternoon, and the sweets and dried fruit on sale make good presents.

The roads across the desert are long, straight and fast, with a lot of truck traffic. Wind and dust can reduce visibility, and distances between towns can be considerable. Spring, in April and May, and autumn are the best seasons, when the temperatures are mild. Summer is fiercely hot and winter nights are freezing.

Check the current rules for foreign motorcyclists before planning a trip to Iran, since they are strict and change often.
t.the persian qanat@34.3,58.7:
In a country where rain is scarce, the people of the Iranian plateau found a way to bring water from the mountains to the plains without pumps. A qanat is a gently sloping underground tunnel, dug by hand from a series of vertical shafts, that taps water in the foothills and carries it by gravity to a village or farm many kilometres away. Evaporation is minimal because the water is underground, and the shafts, ringed with mounds of spoil, mark the line across the desert like a row of volcano craters. UNESCO lists eleven qanats together as The Persian Qanat, and the ones near Gonabad, in the arid east of Khorasan, are among the most famous.

The Gonabad qanat system is often described as among the oldest and deepest in Iran, with a mother well that is said to reach some three hundred metres, and a tunnel that runs for tens of kilometres, though figures vary between sources. Workers called muqannis went down on ropes with picks and oil lamps, and the job was dangerous and skilled, handed from father to son. Qanats shaped Iranian law and community, with water shares measured in hours and sold or inherited, and a village's social life grew around the point where the channel emerged.

For the rider, this is a stark and impressive region. Gonabad sits on the edge of the great salt deserts, with brown mountains to the south and a wide gravel plain, and the roads run straight for kilometres with long views and little traffic outside the towns. Summers are extremely hot, with winds that raise dust, and winters can be bitterly cold, so spring and autumn are best. Pistachio and saffron farms are scattered across the area, and the bright green of the irrigated fields beside the pale ground is a striking contrast.

Gonabad, about eight kilometres away, has some forty-three thousand people, with fuel, bakeries and simple restaurants, and the road to Birjand or Mashhad is lined with service stations at long intervals, so fill up when you can. Ask locally about visiting a working qanat, since some are open to visitors with a guide, and wear sturdy shoes. The water is cold and clear, and a few minutes in the shade of a shaft, listening to the trickle, is one of the great pleasures of desert travel.
t.sarayan@33.9,58.5:
It sits on the edge of the desert, in a basin where irrigation from underground channels allows farms to flourish in a landscape that otherwise looks like Mars, with low, bare, ochre mountains in every direction and a huge sky.

The farms here grow pistachios, barberries, saffron and pomegranates, crops that tolerate heat and poor water, and Iran is the world's leading producer of saffron, much of it from this part of Khorasan. In autumn the saffron crocuses flower for a few weeks, and the fields are picked by hand at dawn, because the petals wilt in the sun. The red stigmas are dried and sold, and a stall in any local market will offer you a tiny packet, with a proud explanation of how to tell the real thing from the fake.

For a rider, the interest is in the emptiness. Roads across the south Khorasan desert run for tens of kilometres without a bend, with the occasional truck stop and police checkpoint, and the temperature changes sharply between day and night. The sky is clear and the stars at night are astonishing. Summer is extremely hot, so plan for spring or autumn, and be careful with fuel, as stations are spaced out and not always supplied. Always top up when you pass one, and carry water, a spare tube and some food.

Roadside teahouses serve strong tea and bread with cheese and walnuts, and the owners tend to be curious and hospitable. Check the foreign-vehicle regulations and permits in advance, since checkpoints in the east of the country are frequent.
t.estancia of la candelaria@-31.1,-64.9:
The Jesuit estancias of Córdoba were farms, mills and chapels that supported the Jesuit college in the city, and La Candelaria is the one that feels most remote. It lies in the dry hills of northern Córdoba province, at the end of a long, quiet approach, with the nearest villages, such as San Carlos, many kilometres away. The ranch house, chapel and workshops stand in a landscape of scrub, rock and grassland, where goats and cattle graze and the silence is complete.

The Jesuits arrived in the area in the late sixteenth century, and by the eighteenth century their estancias were among the most productive agricultural enterprises in the Spanish colonies. They raised cattle, horses and mules, grew wheat and grapes, and ran mills and workshops, with the profits financing the college and university in Córdoba. Labour was provided by Indigenous and enslaved African people, a part of the story that is often overlooked. When King Charles III expelled the Jesuits from the Spanish empire in 1767, the properties were seized and sold. The estancias were declared a World Heritage Site along with the Jesuit Block in Córdoba in 2000.

Reaching it is part of the experience. Roads in this part of Córdoba are a mix of paved highways and gravel tracks, and the final approach may be unpaved, with ruts, loose stones and water crossings in the rainy season. The summer months, from December to March, bring heavy downpours that can make tracks impassable, while winter is dry, cool and clear. Check conditions locally and consider a bike that can handle gravel. Mobile signal can be patchy, so tell someone your route.

There are no services at the estancia itself, so bring water and food. The nearest fuel is at larger towns such as Villa de Soto, around thirty kilometres away, or back in Córdoba, and it is wise to fill up before leaving the main road. Try locro, a hearty stew of corn, beans and meat, and bring a hat, since the sun is strong in the dry hills.
t.jesuit block and estancias of cordoba@-3:
Córdoba is Argentina's second city, a university town of about a million and a half people that has a faintly rebellious reputation. At its centre is the Manzana Jesuítica, the Jesuit Block, a group of buildings from the seventeenth century that includes the church of the Compañía, the old Jesuit college and the university, one of the oldest in the Americas, founded in 1613. The church has a remarkable wooden ceiling shaped like an upturned ship's hull, built by a Flemish Jesuit craftsman, with joinery that shows no nails.

The Jesuits made Córdoba the intellectual capital of colonial Argentina, with a library, printing press and school of theology, and they funded it by running a network of estancias in the surrounding hills. After their expulsion in 1767, the university continued under other orders and later became a secular institution. The 1918 University Reform movement, which began here, spread through Latin America and demanded student participation in university governance. The city is also known for the Cordobazo, a workers' and students' uprising in 1969.

The riding from Córdoba is excellent, with the Sierras Chicas to the north and the high Sierras Grandes to the west. Roads climb out of the city into hills of rock and thorn scrub, past small towns and reservoirs, and along the way you pass estancias at Jesús María and Alta Gracia. At Alta Gracia, the museum of Che Guevara's boyhood home is a popular stop. The weather is dry and sunny in winter, with cool nights, and stormy in summer. City traffic is heavy at rush hour, but the ring road gives quick access to the hills.

Córdoba has fuel stations, mechanics and a wide range of lodging. The student quarter, Nueva Córdoba, has lively cafes and bars. Try an alfajor, a sandwich biscuit with dulce de leche, from a local shop, and a glass of fernet and cola, the city's famous drink. Park the bike in a secure garage, and walk the Jesuit Block with a guide if you can.
t.cordoba@-31.4,-64.2:
Córdoba is Argentina's second city by size and first by claims to learning, a university town where the baroque churches of the Jesuits stand beside student cafés and traffic that never seems to stop. The Jesuits arrived in the sixteenth century and built what is now called the Jesuit Block, a group of church, college and residences that UNESCO listed in 2000. Their university, founded in 1613, is one of the oldest in South America, and in 1918 students here launched a reform movement that spread through Latin American universities. The city is also where Argentines drink fernet with cola, an acquired taste that locals will defend with some force.

For a rider, Córdoba is the start of a classic mountain run. The Camino de las Altas Cumbres leaves the plain and climbs through the Sierras de Córdoba, an old and eroded range, by way of Villa Carlos Paz and its reservoir. Higher up it crosses the Pampa de Achala, a wide grassland plateau at more than two thousand metres where the wind never stops and the cattle graze among granite boulders. The curves between the plateau and Mina Clavero fall quickly, with long views over the valley of Traslasierra, and in the dry season they are a real pleasure.

The mountains have their own wildlife. Andean condors circle on the thermals, and the Quebrada del Condorito National Park nearby protects one of the most reliable places in the country to see them. Weather changes fast. A warm and bright morning in the city can turn into fog, cold wind or a violent summer storm on the heights, so carry layers, and be careful on gravel and wet surfaces. Spring and autumn offer the best conditions, while summer weekends are busy with local families heading for the rivers.

Fuel is easy in the city and in the larger towns on the road, and the roads are paved. Córdoba has excellent food, with locro, empanadas and big grilled meat, and the evening paseo around the old centre goes late. Give yourself a morning to see the Jesuit buildings before the ride begins.
t.cape smokey@46.6,-60.4:
The Cabot Trail has a handful of moments where it stops being a pleasant road and becomes the reason people come, and Cape Smokey is the first of them for anyone riding in from the south. The road climbs about three hundred and sixty metres up the headland, and once it gets above the trees the whole coastline of Cape Breton opens up beneath you, with the Atlantic running out to the horizon and the long arm of Ingonish Beach and Middle Head spread out ahead. On a clear day it reads like a map. On a foggy one it earns its name, as the headland wears a hat of cloud that can swallow the view completely.

Ride it with respect. The climb and the descent have long, sweeping grades, some tight bends, and drop-offs where the guardrail is minimal, and the surface can be patchy after winter frost. Traffic is mostly cars and campervans going slowly, which on a motorcycle means patience, because overtaking points are few and the oncoming views are distracting. Wind from the sea can be fierce at the top, and mornings are often the calmest. Fall is the real prize here, from late September into October, when the hardwood hills turn red and orange, though that is also when traffic peaks for the Celtic Colours festival and fuel and accommodation can get stretched.

The Trail was named for John Cabot, who is traditionally thought to have landed somewhere in this region in 1497, though historians still argue about exactly where. What is certain is that the road itself is much younger, built in the 1920s and 1930s, and that the Cape Breton Highlands National Park, which it winds through, was protected in 1936. Spruce and fir cover the plateau, moose are more common than you might imagine, bald eagles patrol the cliffs, and from the shore you can sometimes see whales offshore in summer.

There is a pull-off for photographs near the summit, and a small provincial park at the foot of the mountain where a short trail leads out along the coast. Ingonish, a few minutes beyond, has fuel, a general store and places to eat; the nearest large town with a wider selection is Baddeck or Sydney, so top up if the tank is low before the long run around the northern cape.
t.gaspe@48.8,-64.5:
Gaspé is a town of around fifteen thousand at the eastern end of Quebec's Gaspé Peninsula, built around a deep bay where, in 1534, Jacques Cartier is said to have come ashore and planted a cross claiming the land for the French king. Mi'kmaq people and Iroquoians of the St Lawrence had long lived and fished here, and the name itself is a Mi'kmaq word for the end of the land. It is a good start for a ride around the peninsula on Route 132, which in this area means a loop of nearly a thousand kilometres right around the coast and back.

The town has a cathedral built of wood, Christ-Roi, which is described as the only wooden cathedral in North America, and a museum on the shore that tells the story of Cartier and the fishermen. It is also the biggest place for a long way, so use it: fill up, buy a coffee and a sandwich, and perhaps eat some of the fresh fish that makes the region's pride. Supplies thin out as you go around the shoreline, with villages stretching along the road every twenty to thirty kilometres.

The riding is easy-going and scenic rather than technical. Route 132 follows the coast beneath the cliffs and over headlands, with long open views across the Gulf of St Lawrence, and sections where it dips right to the water between small fishing villages with red-and-white churches and drying sheds. Just north of Gaspé, Forillon National Park sits at the tip of the peninsula, where the Appalachians finally meet the sea in towering limestone cliffs, and where seals and, in summer, minke and fin whales can be seen offshore. The lighthouse at Cap-des-Rosiers there is the tallest in Canada.

The weather is changeable, with fog rolling in off the cold gulf and strong winds on the headlands, so an extra layer is wise even in July. Summer, from late June to early September, is the best season, while the interior of the peninsula is cooler. Watch for moose at dawn and dusk, which are large enough to wreck a bike and rider alike.
t.perce@48.5,-64.2:
The rock at Percé is one of the most photographed things in eastern Canada, an enormous limestone wall rising out of the Gulf of St Lawrence, hundreds of metres long, with a natural arch at one end cut by waves. Another arch collapsed in the nineteenth century, in 1845, leaving the stack known as the Obelisk beside it, and the whole structure continues to erode slowly. The name means pierced in French, and from the village you can walk across the sandbar at low tide to the foot of it, though checking the tide tables is not optional.

Behind it, a few kilometres offshore, lies Bonaventure Island, which is a bird sanctuary and home to one of the largest colonies of northern gannets in the world, well over a hundred thousand birds nesting on the cliffs and grass in summer. Boats leave from the village harbour and circle the rock and the island, and landing lets you walk to the colony, where the gannets sit a few metres from the path, noisy, white and smelly, and quite unconcerned with you. It is one of the more unusual places I have eaten a sandwich.

On Route 132 the approach from either direction is fine riding, particularly from Gaspé, with the road winding over the hills and dropping to the sea in a series of easy curves. The village of Percé itself is a small tourist town with seafood restaurants, craft shops and guesthouses crowded in the high season, July and August, when traffic crawls and parking is tight, so try for the shoulders of the season, June or September, when the air is cooler and the crowds thin. The larger town of Chandler, about eighty minutes' ride south and with some eight thousand people, offers more fuel and services; you can also fill up in Gaspé.

Fog can hide the rock completely, so you may need patience, and winds from the gulf can be cold. Early morning light on the stone turns it a warm pink and orange, and it is worth getting up for. Take a waterproof layer for the boat.
t.french mountain@46.8,-60.9:
French Mountain is the first great climb on the Cabot Trail as you come up from Chéticamp on the west coast of Cape Breton Island, and it rises to about 455 metres on the plateau of the Cape Breton Highlands. The road climbs steeply in a series of long, powerful bends, with the Gulf of St Lawrence dropping away behind you, and then flattens onto an open, windswept barren of stunted spruce, bogs and low scrub. On a clear day, the view back toward the sea is superb, and on a foggy one you can barely see the verge.

The plateau is a harsh, beautiful place. It is open to the weather, with strong winds, sudden fog and cold rain even in summer, and the vegetation is a tough tundra-like mix of heath, blueberries and tamarack. Moose roam here, and you may see one standing at the edge of the road, a huge, ungainly animal that should be given plenty of room. Black bears also live in the park, and eagles soar overhead.

The road lies within Cape Breton Highlands National Park, and you need a valid park pass if you plan to stop. Fuel is not available on the plateau, so fill the tank at Chéticamp, and carry spare if your bike has a short range. The next services lie at Pleasant Bay, on the far side of the plateau, which is a long way ahead. The road surface is generally good, but frost heaves and patches can be rough, and the descents are steep and tight, so be careful with the brakes.

Coming back through French Mountain on the return leg, you will see the landscape from a new angle, with the light changing and the sea glinting far below. It is a stretch that rewards slow riding, a few stops to take in the view and attention to the weather. Pack waterproofs and a warm layer, and keep an eye on the sky.
t.cheticamp@46.6,-61.0:
Chéticamp is the heart of Acadian Cape Breton, a long, spread-out fishing village on the west coast where French is still the language of the kitchen and the church. The village sits at the foot of the Highlands, with the Gulf of St Lawrence in front and the steep, wooded mountains behind, and its tall steepled church of Saint-Pierre dominates the skyline. Acadian flags, the French tricolour with a gold star, fly from porches and lamp posts, and the houses are painted in bold colours, as if to defy the grey weather.

The village is famous for hooked rugs, a craft that began as a way to use scraps of wool and became a fine art. The patterns are often landscapes, flowers or portraits, and the best ones are works of real skill. A cooperative shop and museum show them off. Music is also part of the culture, with fiddles, step dancing and an annual festival in early autumn, and an evening in a local pub can turn into a session of tunes and songs.

For food, this is the place for seafood chowder, fish cakes, lobster rolls and meat pie, followed by something sweet, such as a molasses cookie. Whale watching boats leave the harbour in summer, and pilot whales and minke whales are often seen close to shore. The beach at Plage Saint-Pierre has warm water by Nova Scotia standards, and a boardwalk and dunes make it a pleasant place for a stroll.

Chéticamp is the western gateway to Cape Breton Highlands National Park, and the Cabot Trail leaves town by climbing steeply onto the plateau. The village has fuel stations, a supermarket and several restaurants, and it is the last reliable place for supplies before the long stretch to Pleasant Bay, so fill the tank and your stomach here. The road in and out is good, but traffic can be heavy in July and August, when tour buses and caravans crowd the route.

Coming back to the village at the end of the day, with the evening sun lighting the church and the smell of the sea in the air, you will understand why people stay. Take time to walk along the harbour, listen to the French spoken around you and let the pace slow down.
t.baddeck@46.1,-60.7:
Baddeck is a small town on the shore of the Bras d'Or Lake, in the middle of Cape Breton Island, and it has a surprising place in the history of flight. Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone, fell in love with the area on a visit in the 1880s and built a summer estate on the headland across the water, which he called Beinn Bhreagh, Gaelic for beautiful mountain. He spent many summers there, and it is where his experiments in kites, hydrofoils and aircraft took place. In February 1909 the Silver Dart, designed by his young engineers, took off from the frozen surface of the lake near Baddeck and flew in the first powered flight in the British Empire.

The Bras d'Or is not a lake in the usual sense. It is an inland sea, an irregular, deep, salt-water basin that connects to the Atlantic through narrow channels, with islands, coves and wooded shores, and tides that are barely noticeable. Sailors prize it for its calm water, and the shores are dotted with white clapboard churches and small farms. The large Mi'kmaq community of Eskasoni lies across the water, a reminder that people lived here long before the Scots arrived.

The town itself is compact, with a main street of craft shops, bakeries, small hotels and a harbour full of sailboats. The Alexander Graham Bell National Historic Site museum sits on a hill above the water, with a large collection of Bell's kites and boats. Kidston Island, close to the shore, has a small lighthouse, and the water around it is calm enough for kayaks.

As a start to the Cabot Trail, Baddeck is the gentle prelude. The road leaves town along the water, then climbs, and by the first hill you can see the lake spread out behind. The surface is generally good, though frost heaves are common in spring, and the road is shared with campers and tour buses in July and August. Fuel stations are in Baddeck itself, and the next reliable stops are on the other side of the island, so fill the tank. Seafood chowder and a pint of local beer are a fitting reward. The best weather is in September, when the forests start to turn, though fog can sweep in off the coast at any time.
t.baddeck@46.1,-60.8:
The Cabot Trail has a reputation to live up to, and its start in Baddeck is the polite part. The loop of about three hundred kilometres around the Cape Breton Highlands was finished in the early 1930s, after years of work, and named after the explorer John Cabot, who sailed along these coasts in 1497, although nobody knows exactly where he landed. The park it circles was created in 1936, and the road is still the main reason most people come. Baddeck is where many riders start, with a tank of fuel and a big breakfast.

The heart of the island is Gaelic. t.charlottetown@46.2,-63.1:

Take a layer, because sea fog and chilly winds are common in the morning, and the Atlantic never quite warms up.
t.joggins fossil cliffs@45.7,-64.4:
Hold a piece of rock from the beach at Joggins and you may be holding a fern that grew three hundred million years ago. The cliffs along this stretch of the Bay of Fundy expose rocks laid down in the Coal Age, the Carboniferous period, when this part of Nova Scotia lay near the equator and was covered in tropical swamp forest. Layer after layer of sandstone, shale and coal runs along the shore for kilometres, and in them are the fossilised trunks of giant trees still standing upright, with the remains of the animals that lived among them. UNESCO listed the site in 2008.

In the nineteenth century, Charles Lyell, the great geologist, visited with John William Dawson, a Nova Scotian, and in 1852 they found the bones of a small reptile inside a hollow tree stump. It was one of the earliest reptiles ever found, later named Hylonomus, and the find fed into the argument about the age of the Earth. Charles Darwin mentioned Joggins in On the Origin of Species, as an example of the slow accumulation of rock.

It has the largest tides in the world, more than ten metres between low and high water, and the sea sweeps in twice a day over the flat mud and sand at the foot of the cliffs. Summer is the best season, and fog and cool wind are common off the bay, even in July. Opening times at the visitor centre change with the season, so check ahead before you make a special trip.
t.mina clavero@-31.7,-65.0:
Mina Clavero is a small river town on the western side of the Sierras de Córdoba, in the long, dry Traslasierra valley, and it is where the Camino de las Altas Cumbres comes to rest after crossing the mountains. The high part is the best part. The Pampa de Achala is a treeless granite plateau where the wind never really stops, the air is thin and cold, and the horizon is a very long way off. Patches of mist can drop over the road in minutes, even in summer, so bring a layer. Near the road is the Quebrada del Condorito, a national park built around a deep canyon where Andean condors still ride the thermals, and with some luck you will see one gliding above the edge. The surface is generally good tarmac, though rock fall, loose gravel and the occasional cow demand attention.

Just along the valley is Villa Cura Brochero, named after José Gabriel Brochero, a priest who spent decades in these hills building roads, schools and a chapel and who was canonised in 2016. Banks, cash machines and cafes cluster along the main street. Prices can change quickly in Argentina, so carry some spare cash.

The best seasons are autumn and spring, when the crowds have gone and the light on the hills is sharp. Summer weekends are busy, and winter can bring frost and even a dusting of snow on the passes.
t.cape north@46.9,-60.5:
Cape North is the place where the Cabot Trail turns and heads for the sea. Moose are numerous and wander onto the road, particularly at dawn and dusk, and bears and bald eagles live in the woods. The best months are July to early October, with the autumn colours at their peak in early October. Early mornings are often foggy and cool. t.copina@-31.6,-64.7:
Copina is a small hill village on the eastern flank of the Sierras de Córdoba, on the road that climbs from the lowlands toward the high plateau, and it is a place where the temperature starts to drop and the road starts to bend. The road, part of the Camino de las Altas Cumbres, is among the best-known mountain roads in Argentina. It climbs from the Punilla valley and Villa Carlos Paz through a series of turns, with long views back over the lowlands, then crosses into the high pampas of the Sierras Grandes. The surface is generally good, with decent tarmac and clear markings, but the road is narrow in places, with steep drops, and the traffic can be heavy at weekends with buses, trucks and holiday cars. Take it carefully, and be ready for sudden fog.

The Sierras de Córdoba are old mountains, much older than the Andes, made of granite and metamorphic rock that has been worn down over hundreds of millions of years. The hills are covered in low shrubs, tussock grass and, in sheltered places, small trees such as the espinillo and the molle. In the early morning, the air smells of wild herbs, and in spring the slopes are dotted with flowers. Birds are plentiful, and the high ground is a place to see the Andean condor soaring on the thermals.

Villa Carlos Paz, about twenty-six kilometres away, is a large lake resort with hotels, restaurants and casinos, and a good place to fill up and eat. The Jesuits built a colonial estancia here in the seventeenth century, and the buildings are a World Heritage Site.

t.pampa de achala@-31.6,-64.8:
The Pampa de Achala is a high plateau at about 2,200 metres, a windswept expanse of grass and granite that sits at the top of the Sierras de Córdoba. After the climb from the lowlands, the landscape changes completely. The trees disappear, the sky grows enormous, and the land rolls away in smooth, bare hills dotted with great grey boulders. t.inzer@54.2,57.6:
Inzer is a small village on the river of the same name, in the Southern Urals of Bashkortostan, and the setting is far more dramatic than the population suggests. The Inzer rises in forested ridges and runs west through narrow valleys cut into limestone and sandstone, with rocky cliffs and pine slopes on either side, and in spring, when the snowmelt swells the river, rafters and kayakers come from across Russia to ride it. Weather is changeable in the mountains: sun and rain can alternate within an hour, and fog may settle in the valleys. Late spring brings flooded rivers and the risk of washouts. The best months are June to September, and autumn is magnificent, with birch and larch turning gold.

Stop on a bridge and watch the water run. The Urals are old mountains, and the river has had plenty of time.
t.abzakovo@53.8,58.6:
Abzakovo is the busiest mountain resort in the Southern Urals, and it is built on a modest scale. A few kilometres from Beloretsk, in the hills where Bashkortostan meets Chelyabinsk Oblast, a cluster of chairlifts, hotels and wooden chalets climbs a forested slope, and from December to April, skiers and snowboarders come from Magnitogorsk, Chelyabinsk and Ufa, which are all within a couple of hours. The surroundings are taiga, with spruce, fir, birch and pine, interspersed with meadows and rocky outcrops. In summer, the hillsides bloom, and in September, the birches turn gold, which is probably the loveliest time of year to visit. Wildlife includes elk, bears and capercaillie, though you are unlikely to see anything but small birds from the road.

The riding is good by the standards of the region, with curving roads that climb through forest and drop into valleys. The approach from Magnitogorsk, to the east, crosses open steppe before the mountains rise, and the final approach is a pleasant sequence of bends. Surface quality varies, with some patched asphalt and frost damage, and the weather is changeable, with fog or rain even in July. Traffic is heavy on winter weekends, when ski buses and cars crowd the road, and quiet in summer. Watch for ice and snow from October to April.

Fuel and food are straightforward enough. Book accommodation in advance for winter weekends.

Stay for the sunset if you can. The hills turn blue and then violet, and the woodsmoke drifts up.
t.magnitogorsk@53.4,59.0:
Magnitogorsk is a city built around a mountain that has been eaten. Magnitnaya Gora, the Magnetic Mountain, was a single hill of almost pure iron ore, so rich that compasses misbehaved nearby, and in 1929 the Soviet government decided to build a giant steelworks beside it as the centrepiece of the first Five-Year Plan. Thousands of workers poured in, living in tents and barracks, while American engineers from the firm of Arthur G. McKee of Cleveland designed the plant on the model of the one at Gary, Indiana. The first blast furnace was lit in 1931, and the city became a symbol of Soviet industrialisation. The American Communist John Scott worked here as a welder and later wrote Behind the Urals, a classic first-hand account.

The steelworks, now one of the largest in the world, still dominates the left bank of the Ural River, and the air can taste of sulphur and metal when the wind is wrong. The city has about four hundred thousand people, in a long strip of wide avenues, with monuments such as the Rear to Front statue, a woman handing a sword to a soldier, commemorating the steel that went into the tanks of the Second World War. The surface is generally good on the main roads, with industrial wear. Weather can be harsh, with fierce winters and hot, dusty summers. The best months are May, June and September. Beloretsk and the Urals proper are a short way west, and the landscape changes quickly into forest and hills.

Fuel is easy, with stations all over the city, and so are food and lodging. Eat a proper meal, and look at the river, steel-grey and slow. Behind the factory chimneys, the old Ural steppe rolls away, windy and wide.
t.zyuratkul@54.9,59.2:

It sits at about seven hundred metres above sea level in a bowl of high ridges, in a national park of the same name, and the water is clear and cold, around three kilometres long, set against dark forest and a skyline of rounded peaks. The ridge behind rises to over a thousand metres, and in autumn the larch and birch on the slopes burn orange and gold against the evergreen.

Elk, brown bear, lynx and capercaillie live here, and the lake attracts ducks and other water birds. The scenery has long drawn visitors, and a few modest guest houses and holiday camps dot the shore, mostly built in the Soviet period, with a simple lakeside feel. It is a peaceful place, and the sound of the wind in the trees is usually the loudest thing around.

Surfaces are variable, with frost heave, gravel and patched tarmac, and you may find the final approach is rough, so go slowly and keep an eye out for animals. Fog and rain are common, and temperatures can drop sharply in the evening, even in July, so pack a warm layer. The best time is probably June to September, with early autumn the most beautiful. Winter brings deep snow and dark days, and the road may be difficult.

For services, think ahead. At the lake, small cafés and shops operate in season, though hours are unpredictable, and you should bring water and a snack. A park entrance fee may apply, and some areas require permission.

Walk down to the shore at dusk. The lake turns the colour of pewter, and the ridges go dark against the sky.
t.cordoba argentina@-31.4,-64.2:

Traffic can be heavy, with fast, chaotic driving, and the streets are a maze of one-way systems, so take care and plan your route. The riverside, the old centre and the park are pleasant to walk in the evening, when the heat of the day fades. Fernet con coca, a mix of the bitter Italian liqueur and cola, is the city's unofficial drink, and you will see it in every bar.

The road west, the Camino de las Altas Cumbres, is the real draw. It climbs through the Sierras Grandes, passing from farmland and scrub to high grassland and rock, reaching over two thousand metres. The surface is paved and good, with long, graceful bends and wide views over the plains. Weather can change fast, with fog and cloud on the heights and sudden storms in summer, so carry a waterproof. Spring and autumn give the best conditions, with clear air and comfortable temperatures.

If you have time, wander through the old quarter, where the cathedral, with its mix of colonial and baroque features, and the Cabildo, the old town hall, face the main square. Look into the Jesuit church and the university library for a sense of the city's long intellectual history. Eat an empanada or a plate of locro, and take a seat in a cafe. It is a city with a lot of character, and it gives a good start to a ride into the mountains.
t.merlo san luis@-32.3,-65.0:
Merlo is a small resort town of about eleven thousand people on the western side of the Sierra de los Comechingones, a long, rounded range of mountains that marks the border between the provinces of Córdoba and San Luis. Whatever the science, the claim is easy to believe on a sunny afternoon, when the air is dry, the sky is blue and the temperature is soft.

The ride over the mountains from Mina Clavero is the highlight. The road climbs from the Córdoba side through grassland and rock outcrops, crosses the crest and then descends in long bends through increasingly dry scrub toward the San Luis plain. The surface is generally good, though there are patches of broken asphalt, and the gradients are steady. Fog and cloud can settle on the crest, particularly in the morning, so keep an eye on the sky. The best time is spring and autumn, with clear light and comfortable temperatures, while summer is hot in the valley and brings afternoon storms.

Merlo has everything a traveller needs: fuel, repair shops, supermarkets, restaurants and a wide range of hotels and cabins. The main street and the plaza are lively in the evenings, with craft stalls, cafes and ice cream parlours, and the pace of life is relaxed. Local food leans on grilled meat, empanadas and goat dishes, while the regional sweets, made with figs, quince and dulce de leche, make good gifts. Concarán and Santa Rosa del Conlara, both smaller towns, lie to the north and offer a quieter view of rural life.

Condors ride the thermals above the peaks, and in the lower valleys, algarrobo trees, a kind of mesquite, provide shade and a fruit that was once ground into flour. Cerro Champaquí, the highest peak in the region, rises to the northeast, and on a clear day you can pick it out above the other summits. It is a gentle, sunny corner of Argentina, and a fine place to slow down.
t.estancia of alta gracia@-31.7,-64.4:
Alta Gracia sits where the Córdoba plains begin to buckle into the Sierras Chicas, and its Jesuit estancia is the reason the town exists. The Jesuits established the estate in the seventeenth century, and by the eighteenth it was a thriving enterprise: a church, a residence around a cloister, workshops, and an ingenious dam with a reservoir feeding irrigation canals. It was part of the great network of Jesuit properties around Córdoba, collectively a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000, which funded the university and college in the city.

When the Jesuits were expelled from Spanish territories in 1767, the estancia passed through various hands. One of them belonged to Santiago de Liniers, the Spanish officer who led the defence of Buenos Aires against the British and became viceroy. In the twentieth century the town drew other names: the composer Manuel de Falla spent his last years in Alta Gracia, and the young Ernesto Guevara grew up in a house here, now a museum. Few small towns carry so many stories at once.

The ride from Córdoba takes you southwest on good roads, through suburbs and then open country, with the sierras rising ahead in blue folds. Alta Gracia is a town of around forty thousand, with fuel, banks, restaurants and plenty of cafés around the plaza, so practical needs are no trouble at all. The surrounding hills offer winding roads and reservoirs, with plenty of lookouts, and the climate is comfortable most of the year. Summer afternoons can bring sharp storms; winters are dry, with clear, cold mornings.

Try the regional food, such as empanadas, locro on cold days and a thick, sweet dulce de leche, and take time to walk the old estancia grounds. The clock tower, the church and the tranquil reservoir make a satisfying morning. If you are lucky enough to be here on a quiet weekday, the shade of the old trees and the smell of wood smoke create a strong sense of the past.
t.estancia of santa catalina@-30.9,-64.2:
The Jesuits were more than priests. In seventeenth-century Córdoba, in the heart of what is now Argentina, they ran a university, a network of missions and a string of estancias, ranches whose profits paid for their schools. UNESCO lists it with the other Jesuit Block and Estancias of Córdoba. The rooms are plain and thick-walled, with deep verandas, tiled floors and heavy wooden doors, and in the summer heat the shade in the courtyard is as good as any sermon. From Jesús María, the nearest town of some size and home to another Jesuit estancia with a wine tradition, you climb into rolling pasture and rocky hills, with a quiet road that passes small farms, eucalyptus windbreaks and long views toward the sierra. The surface is mostly paved, though cracked in places, with gentle curves, and the traffic is light. Dust and gravel appear on the side roads, and sudden afternoon storms in summer, between November and March, can be violent. Autumn and spring are lovely and dry, with a clear light.

La Granja, closer in distance, is a small hill town, but for fuel and a proper meal Jesús María is the better stop, with several stations and traditional parrillas. Try a locro stew in cold months, or grilled meat with provoleta cheese. Entry to the estancia is by ticket, with limited hours, and midday is when the quiet is deepest. Bring water, since there are few services in between, and plan to reach the estancia in the morning, when the light on the white walls is best.
t.qanat of baladeh@34.1,58.4:
Qanats are one of the great quiet inventions of human history, and the Persian ones are the best. A qanat is an underground channel that carries water from an aquifer in the foothills to a village in the desert, using nothing but gravity, with a line of vertical shafts every few dozen metres to let the diggers in and out and to let air in. The technique appeared in Iran about three thousand years ago, and in the dry plateaus of the interior it made agriculture and cities possible. The work was done by hand, by specialists called muqannis, who handed down their skills through families and had their own guild. t.st peters bay@46.4,-62.6:

t.east point@46.5,-62.0:

t.souris@46.4,-62.2:

t.alma@45.6,-64.9:

t.ganjali khan@30.3,57.1:

t.ufa@54.7,56.0:

t.fakhr abad@34.7,58.1:
So this text is about the country around it, which is large, dry and old.

t.qasabeh gonabad@34.3,58.7:

t.beloretsk@54.0,58.4:

t.sterlitamak@53.6,55.9:

t.nugush@53.0,56.4:
